method.metaTitle: IQode Method — 5 Steps of Thinking · IQode Lab
method.metaDescription: IQode Method is a 5-step thinking framework designed by IQode Lab — integrating Project-Based Learning, Design Thinking, Computational Thinking and Reflective Learning.

hero.title: 5 Steps of Thinking
hero.subtitle: Not a teaching process. A thinking framework children carry for life.
hero.tagline: IQode Lab · Build thinking, not just coding

intro.heading: What is IQode Method?
intro.body: IQode Method is a 5-step thinking framework designed exclusively by IQode Lab — integrating scientifically proven educational foundations: Project-Based Learning, Design Thinking, Computational Thinking, Constructionism (Papert), and Reflective Learning.
intro.coreDef: These 5 steps do not change session by session. What changes is the problem, the difficulty level, and the teacher's questions. Children usually don't realize they are following 5 steps — they just see themselves solving an interesting problem without knowing the answer until they find it themselves. This is the state of self-directed learning.
intro.sdtIntro: Each step in IQode Method corresponds to a basic psychological need according to Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2020) — together creating conditions for children to shift from extrinsic motivation to intrinsic motivation.

why.heading: Why did IQode Method come about?
why.body: The STEM and Coding market for children is very crowded — but most focus on tools (Scratch, mBot, Python) rather than thinking. Students finish and know how to use Scratch, but don't know how to think. They can assemble a robot, but don't know how to debug. They can complete template exercises, but get stuck on unfamiliar problems.
why.q1: Does the center teach children what to do, or how to think?
why.a1: The thinking process matters more than the final product
why.q2: When a child encounters an error, what does the teacher do?
why.a2: How errors are handled reveals the true teaching philosophy
why.q3: Is the child allowed to design their own solution, or follow a template?
why.a3: Autonomy determines the level of thinking development
why.q4: After the course, what new capabilities will the child have?
why.a4: Thinking outcomes matter more than tool certificates
why.unescoBody: According to the UNESCO AI Competency Framework (2024), in the age of AI, the three most important competencies are not knowing how to use AI tools — but: critical thinking, information evaluation, and self-regulated learning. These are precisely what IQode Method builds.

step1.label: STEP 01
step1.name: REAL PROBLEM
step1.tagline: Start from what children will actually encounter in real life
step1.psychBody: In educational psychology, this is called Relatedness — one of the three basic psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory. When children realize "this problem happens in my life," their brain no longer classifies it as "studying" — but as "solving a real problem." And people don't need reminders to solve their own problems.
step1.scienceNote: Challenge Based Learning (2025): "Students don't need to be motivated because they genuinely want to solve the problem." This happens when the problem has real meaning for the learner.
step1.do1: Choose problems with specific situations, close to the daily life of children that age — not vague "academic" scenarios.
step1.do2: Ask questions so children self-connect the problem to their own experience before explaining: "Have you ever encountered this before?"
step1.do3: Keep the problem open enough that children don't know what the outcome will be — the element of surprise stimulates curiosity.
step1.dont1: Don't explain "this problem is meaningful because..." yourself — children must feel it, not be persuaded.
step1.dont2: Don't use purely hypothetical problems with no connection to the child's reality.
step1.dont3: Don't reveal the answer or solution direction upfront — even when children ask.
step1.q1: "Have you ever encountered this problem before?"
step1.q2: "What would you need to know to solve this?"
step1.q3: "Why do you think people need to solve this problem?"

step2.label: STEP 02
step2.name: ANALYZE
step2.tagline: Understand the problem before touching any tool
step2.psychBody: This step builds Metacognition — the ability to self-check whether you understand. Children cannot self-learn if they don't know whether they are understanding or blindly following. When a teacher asks a child to "re-explain the problem in their own words" without looking at it, the brain is forced to evaluate: "Do I truly understand, or am I just recalling the problem statement?"
step2.scienceNote: Education Endowment Foundation (EEF, UK): Metacognition & Self-Regulation is the highest-impact teaching strategy for improving learning outcomes. Students taught metacognition strategies improve results in Literacy, Math and Science.
step2.do1: Ask children to close the problem and re-explain it in their own language — not read it back.
step2.do2: Listen to how children explain to detect gaps in understanding — not just misunderstandings.
step2.do3: If children can't explain: don't re-explain — ask smaller sub-questions for them to discover on their own.
step2.dont1: Don't let children pass this step when they just say "I understand" without being able to explain specifically.
step2.dont2: Don't correct immediately when children explain incorrectly — ask: "Are you sure? Try explaining that part again."
step2.dont3: Don't do it for them — even under time pressure. Skipping this step is the main reason children follow along without understanding why.
step2.q1: "Don't look at the problem — tell me the problem in your own words."
step2.q2: "What does the computer need to know to solve this problem?"
step2.q3: "Which part are you not sure about?"
step2.q4: "Can you explain that step to a friend who has never learned this?"

step3.label: STEP 03
step3.name: DESIGN
step3.psychBody: Autonomy in Self-Determination Theory doesn't mean "freedom to do anything." It means: children feel they are the active designer — not copying someone else. When children draw their own diagram by hand, that product belongs to them. They will want to protect and improve what they created themselves — and easily discard what they only copied.
step3.scienceNote: Constructionism (Papert, 1980): learners learn most deeply when they create their own products, not copying templates. Autonomy is the psychological need most harmed by imposing answers.
step3.do1: Require children to draw a diagram on paper BEFORE opening any tool.
step3.do2: Only ask small guiding questions — don't draw a sample, don't point at the paper.
step3.do3: Accept many different ways of drawing — there is no single "correct" diagram. The internal logic is what matters.
step3.dont1: Don't draw a sample — even just as a "hint." When teachers draw, children look and copy, not design independently.
step3.dont2: Don't mark right/wrong too early — let children discover through questions.
step3.dont3: Don't skip this step because it "wastes time." This is the step children learn how to think — not how to code.
step3.q1: "Before coding, draw it out: what does the machine need to know? What order should the machine follow?"
step3.q2: "If the problem changed slightly, would your diagram need to change?"
step3.q3: "Is there any case you haven't accounted for in your diagram?"

step4.label: STEP 04
step4.name: BUILD
step4.tagline: Use tools to verify — not to find the answer
step4.psychBody: Competence in SDT is the feeling of "I can do this" — not from teacher praise, but from seeing your logic run correctly. When children code to verify the logic they designed (not to find the answer), each time the code runs correctly is concrete evidence: "My thinking is right." This is the foundation of genuine confidence.
step4.scienceNote: Project-Based Learning (meta-analysis, Frontiers in Psychology 2023, 66 studies): compared to traditional instruction, PBL significantly improves thinking skills, learning attitudes and academic outcomes. Important: when code is wrong it's INFORMATION — the logic has a flaw.
step4.do1: Remind children: "Code is to test whether the logic you just designed runs correctly — not to find the answer."
step4.do2: When code is wrong: "What is the code doing? What does your diagram say the machine should do? Do they match?"
step4.do3: Encourage reading error messages and guessing before asking the teacher.
step4.dont1: Don't fix children's code — even as a "hint" by pointing at the error line.
step4.dont2: Don't praise "Well done!" when code runs correctly — replace with: "What did you just verify?"
step4.dont3: Don't let children try randomly — always require them to explain their reasoning before changing any line.
step4.right2: "If you change X, what will the result be?"
step4.right3: "Is there a way to make the code run faster?"
step4.wrong1: "What is the code doing differently from your diagram?"
step4.wrong2: "What hint do you see in this error message?"
step4.wrong3: "Which part do you want to fix first? Why?"
step4.q1: "What is the code doing? What does your diagram say the machine should do?"
step4.q2: "What hint do you see in this error message?"
step4.q3: "Which part do you want to try fixing first? Why?"

step5.label: STEP 05
step5.name: REFLECT
step5.tagline: Look back at how you thought — not just the result
step5.psychBody: The first four steps build problem-solving skills. Step 5 builds the skill of learning from one's own experience — this is the meta-skill: learning how to learn. Children can sustain self-learning not because they are talented, but because they know how to look back at their thinking process and draw lessons for next time.
step5.scienceNote: Reflective Learning — Schön (1983) and the Reflective Practitioner: self-reflection after each activity helps build growth mindset and the ability to self-improve over time. The four tiers of Reflect in IQode Method progressively build Metacognitive Monitoring and Optimization Thinking.
step5.t1q: "Don't look at your notes — retell from beginning to end everything you did today."
step5.t1skill: Episodic Memory + Self-Monitoring: knowing what you went through. If you can retell → you truly understood.
step5.t2q: "What logic solved this problem? Next time you encounter a similar problem, where will you start?"
step5.t2skill: Schematic Learning: building reusable "thinking templates" for future use.
step5.t3q: "What specifically felt difficult? How did you handle it?"
step5.t3skill: Difficulty Awareness: turning difficulty into experience, not an obstacle.
step5.t4q: "The way you just did it and another way — what are the pros and cons of each?"
step5.t4skill: Optimization Thinking: engineering mindset — not just finding an answer, but finding the best answer.
step5.dont1: Don't praise "You learned so well today" — praise creates dependence on external evaluation, destroying exactly what Reflect is building.
step5.dont2: Don't summarize the lesson for children — a teacher who summarizes is the teacher who is learning, not the child.
step5.dont3: Don't force all 4 tiers every session — read each child's state. Sometimes going deep on Tier 2 is better than rushing through Tier 4.
step5.condition: A maximum of 5–6 students per class is a necessary condition for Reflect to happen properly. With large classes, teachers don't have enough time and attention to read each child's state and adjust the depth of each tier.
step5.q1: "Don't look at your notes — retell from beginning to end everything you did today."
step5.q2: "Next time you encounter a similar problem, where will you start?"
step5.q3: "Is there a way to do this faster or better?"

about.metaTitle: About IQode Lab · Our Story & Team
about.metaDescription: IQode Lab is an edu-tech startup teaching computational thinking to kids 6–17. We build logical thinking and problem-solving skills, not just syntax.

hero.title: About IQode Lab
hero.subtitle: We believe learning to code isn't about making every child a developer. It's the best way to train Logical Thinking and Problem-Solving Skills — skills that survive the AI era.

story.heading: An edtech startup born from genuine passion
story.body1: IQode Lab was founded by software engineers with a burning question: why do most Vietnamese students learn programming but still can't solve simple real-world problems?
story.body2: The answer: because we teach language, not thinking. IQode Lab was created to change that.

pillars.heading: 4 Pillars of Educational Philosophy
pillars.p1Desc: Apply logical thinking to solve real-world problems. Every challenge is solvable when you reason in the right direction.
pillars.p2Desc: Break problems down — define each phase — map solutions. The skill to split large problems into manageable parts.
pillars.p3Desc: Build the habit of self-study, self-debug, and self-improvement — no waiting. The most important skill in a rapidly evolving industry.
pillars.p4Desc: Every skill is aimed at creating real products and value. Students don't just know theory — they build things that work.
